newsitem.title: USA: Slovenia may consider investment abroad - minister.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia may consider investment abroad - minister.

text.p: Slovenia may consider investing abroad to reduce the pressure on the country's monetary system put by foreign capital inflows, said Marjan Senjur, Slovenian Minister of Economic Relations and Development.
Almost like the embarrassment of the riches, Slovenia's economic success attracted too great an influx of "hot money," Senjur told Reuters in an interview.
"The monetary problems still exists," he said. "We should think how to export capital -- how to stimulate investment abroad."
Slovenia is the only central European country with credit rated Single A by Standard and Poor's and A3 by Moody's.

"Our central bank had to restrict inflows of foreign capital out of monetary reasons," he said, noting that the inflows had reached an alarming proportion in the second half of last year, inflating the money suppy and pushing up the value of its currency.
The Bank of Slovenia recently introduced new regulations requiring that transactions be made through special custody accounts opened at a domestic bank.
But the custody account is not enough of a deterrent, Senjur said, adding that he expected the foreign short-term investments to resume as investors began adapting to the new rules.

Admitting that the banks charged "too high a price" for the custodial services, which add 10 to 15 percent of cost to foreign investors, Senjur said the government is not considering putting a ceiling on the fees.
Senjur said he did not think the Slovenian currency, the tolar, is overvalued, despite complaints by exporters.
In 1996, the tolar appreciated against the German mark, but did not appreciate against the U.S. dollar, he said.
About 60 percent of Slovenia's gross domestic product derives from export.
Sterlization to keep the tolar from further appreciation was considered "costly," according to Senjur because it would push up domestic interest rates and depress the economy.
Senjur was in New York to meet U.S. investors at the Central European Free Trade Agreement conference organized by the Business Council for International Understanding.
